analysis.one_liner: Bars executive agencies from mass-canceling federal student loan debt.
analysis.headline: The bill drew one sponsor and three Republican cosponsors, was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit the Departments of Education, Treasury, and Justice from taking any action to cancel or forgive federal student loan balances on a mass scale, covering FFEL, Direct, Perkins, and health-education loans — including loans made in the future. It would keep only the targeted forgiveness programs that were already finalized in regulation as of March 12, 2020. Any broader relief would require a new act of Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who repaid their loans or never attended college would avoid absorbing the cost of mass cancellation, which the bill's own findings call unfair. The federal government would keep collecting payments and interest on every covered loan. Loan servicers and debt collectors would keep the business of managing and pursuing those balances, since the bill applies to loans made before or after enactment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Non-borrowing taxpayers and loan servicing firms

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the Education, Treasury, and Justice Departments from taking any action to cancel or forgive the outstanding balances of covered loans — FFEL, Direct, Perkins, and Health Education Assistance loans — including loans made after enactment.
Carves out targeted federal forgiveness, cancellation, and repayment programs that were carried out under the Higher Education Act and already in final regulation on March 12, 2020.
States its fairness rationale in the findings: Congress declares it unfair for taxpayers who paid off their loans or never attended college to pay for those who chose to take out student loans.

Bars agencies from issuing or publishing any regulation that goes beyond what statute and regulation allowed on March 12, 2020, unless it reflects the clear intent of Congress — keeping debt-relief decisions with Congress rather than the executive branch.

analysis.who_pays: Borrowers holding the covered federal loans would bear the full cost: they would keep repaying balances that a mass cancellation would have erased, and any future relief would require Congress to pass a new law — no such law was pending. The bill offers nothing in exchange: no lower tuition, no easier repayment terms, no debt reduction of any kind.

drawbacks.text: Borrowers get no relief and no alternative: the bill blocks executive cancellation of covered loans but contains no provision lowering college costs or reducing anyone's debt.

The design is frozen in time: agencies could not adapt or expand relief beyond what regulations allowed on March 12, 2020, so responding to a new recession or emergency would require new legislation first.

The taxpayer savings supporters point to come entirely from borrowers continuing to pay — not from any program change — so the bill's entire effect is to take a form of relief off the table for the people holding the covered loans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: An honest supporter would say the bill protects the federal budget, respects Congress's control over loan terms, and honors the people who already repaid or never borrowed — all real. But the savings come only by leaving borrowers' balances untouched, and the bill is a prohibition rather than a policy: it does nothing about why student debt is high or how it should be repaid. For the borrowers the covered loans span, the bill's only effect would be to foreclose relief, which makes the cost side heavy and the benefit side diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, never got a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott DesJarlais introduced the bill on June 15, 2022, joined by Reps. Ashley Hinson, John Rose, and Michael Cloud as original cosponsors; no other member ever signed on.
The Speaker referred it the same day to the Education and Labor Committee and, for parts within its jurisdiction, to the Energy and Commerce Committee.
Neither committee took it up: the action record shows nothing after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill declared that Congress had never given the executive branch authority to cancel student loans on a mass scale and sought to make that permanent by statute, freezing permissible agency action to the rules in effect on March 12, 2020.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal student loan borrowers came out ahead. The bill died without a vote, leaving the executive branch free to pursue mass cancellation — which President Biden announced by executive action months later, the very action this bill was written to prohibit.

for.name: Scott DesJarlais
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 15, 2022; took no further recorded action on it.

for.name: Ashley Hinson, John Rose, and Michael Cloud
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; they were the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the record shows no action after the June 2022 committee referrals.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which sat in his committee from referral until the Congress ended.

against.name: Joe Biden
against.what_they_did: Announced a plan in August 2022 to cancel up to $20,000 in federal student debt per borrower by executive action — the kind of mass cancellation this bill was drafted to prohibit.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and in the Democratic-run House the bill never reached a vote.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and collection agencies
industries.note: Mass cancellation would erase the balances these firms are paid to service and pursue. By keeping every covered loan payable — including loans made in the future — the bill would preserve their revenue base, and borrowers would keep paying.

industries.industry: Federal government as student loan creditor (Education and Treasury Departments)
industries.note: The government would keep collecting payments and interest on all covered loans, protecting federal revenues and the budget. That gain comes directly out of borrowers' pockets, though non-borrowing taxpayers share in avoiding the cost of cancellation.
